segments.text: Here are tiny glowing beads, each one far smaller than the wavelength of light.
segments.say: Here are tiny glowing beads, each one far smaller than the wavelength of light.

segments.text: Now look at them through a perfect microscope. Every bead has become a soft disc, wrapped in faint rings.
segments.say: Now look at them through a perfect microscope. Every bead has become a soft disc, wrapped in faint rings.

segments.text: Push two beads closer than about 200 nanometres, and they merge into a single blob.
segments.say: Push two beads closer than about two hundred nanometres, and they merge into a single blob.

segments.text: No lens maker can fix this. So why can't even a perfect lens make a perfect point?
segments.say: No lens maker can fix this. So why can't even a perfect lens, make a perfect point?

segments.text: First, what is an image? Think of any object as a crowd of tiny points of light.
segments.say: First, what is an image? Think of any object as a crowd of tiny points of light.

segments.text: A lens turns each point into the same small blur, called the point spread function, or PSF.
segments.say: A lens turns each point into the same small blur, called the point spread function, or P S F.

segments.text: Each point stamps a copy of the PSF at its own position, scaled by its brightness. The beads glow independently, so the stamps simply add.
segments.say: Each point stamps a copy of the P S F at its own position, scaled by its brightness. The beads glow independently, so the stamps simply add.

segments.text: Adding up shifted copies like this is called a convolution. The image is the object, convolved with the PSF.
segments.say: Adding up shifted copies like this is called a convolution. The image is the object, convolved with the P S F.

segments.text: Now feed the blur a single wave, a pattern of stripes. Out comes the same wave, only fainter.
segments.say: Now feed the blur a single wave, a pattern of stripes. Out comes the same wave, only fainter.

segments.text: Just like propagation in episode one, waves are the eigenvectors of blurring. In the Fourier basis, convolution becomes multiplication.
segments.say: Just like propagation in episode one, waves are the eigenvectors of blurring. In the Fourier basis, convolution becomes multiplication.

segments.text: Each spatial frequency kx just gets multiplied by one number: the transfer function, the Fourier transform of the PSF.
segments.say: Each spatial frequency, kay ex, just gets multiplied by one number: the transfer function, the Fourier transform of the P S F.

segments.text: Notice how fine stripes fade much more than coarse ones.
segments.say: Notice how fine stripes fade much more than coarse ones.

segments.text: So where does the PSF come from? Recall episode one: any light field is a sum of plane waves.
segments.say: So where does the P S F come from? Recall episode one: any light field is a sum of plane waves.

segments.text: A point sends them out in every direction, each with its own kx = k sin θ. Together they fill the k-circle.
segments.say: A point sends them out in every direction, each with its own kay ex, equal to kay sine theta. Together, they fill the kay circle.

segments.text: But a lens has a finite opening. It only catches waves tilted less than some largest angle.
segments.say: But a lens has a finite opening. It only catches waves tilted less than some largest angle.

segments.text: The sine of that angle is the numerical aperture, NA. On the k-circle, the lens keeps just a cap: kx up to k times NA.
segments.say: The sine of that angle is the numerical aperture, N.A. On the kay circle, the lens keeps just a cap: kay ex up to kay times NA.

segments.text: Waves with kx beyond k are evanescent: they never even leave the object. So the lens is a hole in k-space, called the pupil.
segments.say: Waves with kay ex beyond kay are evanescent: they never even leave the object. So the lens is a hole in kay space, called the pupil.

segments.text: Add up only the waves that pass through this hole, and you get the PSF. Watch what happens as the aperture opens.
segments.say: Add up only the waves that pass through this hole, and you get the P S F. Watch what happens as the aperture opens.

segments.text: The cap widens, and the spot shrinks. Its bright core, the Airy disc, has a radius of 0.61 λ/NA.
segments.say: The cap widens, and the spot shrinks. Its bright core, the Airy disc, has a radius of zero point six one, lambda over NA.

segments.text: And magnification can't save you: zooming in on the image only gives you a bigger blur.
segments.say: And magnification can't save you: zooming in on the image only gives you a bigger blur.

segments.text: In 1873, Ernst Abbe asked a sharper question: what is the finest grating a lens can image?
segments.say: In eighteen seventy three, Ernst Ahbuh asked a sharper question: what is the finest grating a lens can image?

segments.text: A grating of period d splits a plane wave into a straight beam and two first orders, tilted at sin θ = ±λ/d.
segments.say: A grating of period dee splits a plane wave into a straight beam, and two first orders, tilted at sine theta equals plus or minus lambda over dee.

segments.text: The lens must catch the straight beam and at least one first order: their interference rebuilds the stripes.
segments.say: The lens must catch the straight beam, and at least one first order: their interference rebuilds the stripes.

segments.text: Now make the grating finer. The orders tilt further out, and once they leave the cap, the stripes are gone.
segments.say: Now make the grating finer. The orders tilt further out, and once they leave the cap, the stripes are gone.

segments.text: So with straight-on light, the finest period a lens can image is λ/NA.
segments.say: So with straight on light, the finest period a lens can image is lambda over NA.

segments.text: Abbe's trick: tilt the illumination, so the straight beam enters at one edge of the cap. Now a first order fits in at the other edge.
segments.say: Ahbuh's trick: tilt the illumination, so the straight beam enters at one edge of the cap. Now a first order fits in, at the other edge.

segments.text: That doubles the reach, to a finest period of λ/2NA. This is the diffraction limit.
segments.say: That doubles the reach, to a finest period of lambda over two NA. This is the diffraction limit.

segments.text: Abbe's picture is for coherent light, like a laser, where fields add: the pupil cuts the field off sharply at k·NA.
segments.say: Ahbuh's picture is for coherent light, like a laser, where fields add: the pupil cuts the field off sharply, at kay times NA.

segments.text: Glowing beads are different: each emits with its own random, ever-changing phase, so intensities add, not fields.
segments.say: Glowing beads are different: each emits with its own random, ever changing phase, so intensities add, not fields.

segments.text: Then the transfer function, called the OTF, is the overlap of the pupil with a shifted copy of itself.
segments.say: Then the transfer function, called the O T F, is the overlap of the pupil with a shifted copy of itself.

segments.text: Slide one copy across the other. The overlap shrinks smoothly, and only reaches zero at twice the coherent cutoff.
segments.say: Slide one copy across the other. The overlap shrinks smoothly, and only reaches zero at twice the coherent cutoff.

segments.text: So incoherent light reaches twice as far in kx. But it isn't simply better: its contrast fades toward the cutoff.
segments.say: So incoherent light reaches twice as far in kay ex. But it isn't simply better: its contrast fades toward the cutoff.

segments.text: Here's one test chart, imaged both ways. Coherent light rings at every edge; incoherent light is smooth, but its finest spokes wash out.
segments.say: Here's one test chart, imaged both ways. Coherent light rings at every edge. Incoherent light is smooth, but its finest spokes wash out.

segments.text: On a computer, imaging is the same three steps as in episode one: FFT, multiply by the OTF, inverse FFT.
segments.say: On a computer, imaging is the same three steps as in episode one: F F T, multiply by the O T F, and inverse F F T.

segments.text: So can we run it backwards? Take a blurred image with a little camera noise, and divide by the OTF.
segments.say: So can we run it backwards? Take a blurred image with a little camera noise, and divide by the O T F.

segments.text: Disaster. Wherever the OTF is tiny, the noise gets multiplied by thousands, and swamps everything.
segments.say: Disaster. Wherever the O T F is tiny, the noise gets multiplied by thousands, and swamps everything.

segments.text: The Wiener filter is the stable version. It divides where the signal beats the noise, and gently gives up where it doesn't.
segments.say: The Wiener filter is the stable version. It divides where the signal beats the noise, and gently gives up where it doesn't.

segments.text: But beyond the cutoff, the OTF is exactly zero. Those details never reached the camera, and no filter can bring them back.
segments.say: But beyond the cutoff, the O T F is exactly zero. Those details never reached the camera, and no filter can bring them back.

segments.text: Only prior knowledge or extra measurements can fill them in. And that's where computational imaging begins.
segments.say: Only prior knowledge, or extra measurements, can fill them in. And that's where computational imaging begins.

segments.text: So here is the whole idea. Imaging is convolution with the PSF.
segments.say: So here is the whole idea. Imaging is convolution with the P S F.

segments.text: A lens only keeps directions with sin θ ≤ NA, so details finer than about λ/2NA never arrive.
segments.say: A lens only keeps directions with sine theta up to NA, so details finer than about lambda over two NA never arrive.

segments.text: One honest caveat: real lenses blur differently away from the centre, so the PSF slowly changes across the field.
segments.say: One honest caveat: real lenses blur differently away from the centre, so the P S F slowly changes across the field.

segments.text: And we saw that intensities add for glowing beads. But why? When does light interfere, and when doesn't it?
segments.say: And we saw that intensities add for glowing beads. But why? When does light interfere, and when doesn't it?
